title: Part 4, Chapter 2
paragraphs: It was nearly eight o'clock. The two young men hurried to Bakaleyev's to arrive before Luzhin.
"Who was that?" Razumihin asked as soon as they were in the street.

"It was Svidrigaïlov, that landowner in whose house my sister was insulted when she was their governess. He drove her out through his unwanted attentions—Marfa Petrovna, his wife, was behind it. This same Marfa Petrovna later begged Dounia's forgiveness, and now she's suddenly died. We were talking about her this morning. I don't know why, but I'm afraid of that man. He came here straight after his wife's funeral. He's very strange and is determined to do something. We must protect Dounia from him—that's what I wanted to tell you. Do you hear?"
"Protect her! What can he do to Avdotya Romanovna? Thank you for telling me, Rodya. We will, we'll protect her! Where does he live?"
"I don't know."
"Why didn't you ask? What a pity! I'll find out, though."
"Did you see him?" Raskolnikov asked after a pause.
"Yes, I noticed him. I got a good look."
"You really saw him? Saw him clearly?" Raskolnikov pressed.
"Yes, I remember him perfectly. I'd know him among a thousand. I have a good memory for faces."
They walked in silence for a while.
"Hmm, that's good," Raskolnikov muttered. "Because, you know, I thought—I keep thinking it might have been a hallucination."
"What do you mean? I don't follow."
"Well, you all say," Raskolnikov went on, twisting his lips into a smile, "that I'm mad. It occurred to me just now that perhaps I really am mad and only saw a phantom."
"What are you saying?"
"Who can tell? Maybe I really am mad, and everything that's happened these last few days is just my imagination."
"Oh, Rodya, you've been upset again! But what did he say? Why did he come?"
Raskolnikov didn't answer. Razumihin thought for a moment.

"Now let me tell you my story," he began. "I came to you—you were asleep. Then we had dinner, and I went to Porfiry's. Zametov was still there. I tried to get started but couldn't find the right approach. They don't seem to understand and can't understand, but they're not the least bit embarrassed. I took Porfiry aside by the window and tried to talk, but it was still hopeless. He looked away and I looked away. Finally I shook my fist in his ugly face and told him that as his relative I'd smash his skull. He just stared at me. I cursed and left. That was all. Very stupid. To Zametov I said nothing. But you see, I thought I'd made a mess of it. Then on the way downstairs a brilliant idea hit me: why should we care? If you were in any danger, that would be different. But why should you care a fig? You're not connected to any of it. We'll have a laugh at them later. If I were you, I'd baffle them even more. How ashamed they'll be afterward! Hang them! We can give them a thrashing later, but for now let's just laugh at them!"

"To be sure," Raskolnikov answered. "But what will you say tomorrow?" he thought. Strange to say, until that moment it had never occurred to him to wonder what Razumihin would think when he found out. As the thought struck him, Raskolnikov looked at his friend. Razumihin's account of his visit to Porfiry held very little interest for him now. So much had come and gone since then.

In the corridor they ran into Luzhin. He had arrived punctually at eight and was looking for the room number, so all three went in together without greeting or looking at one another. The young men entered first, while Pyotr Petrovitch, with exaggerated propriety, lingered in the passage removing his coat. Pulcheria Alexandrovna came forward at once to greet him in the doorway. Dounia was welcoming her brother. Pyotr Petrovitch walked in and bowed to the ladies quite amiably, though with heightened dignity. He looked rather put out, however, as though he hadn't yet recovered his composure. Pulcheria Alexandrovna, apparently somewhat embarrassed herself, hurriedly seated everyone around the round table where a samovar was boiling. Dounia and Luzhin sat facing each other across the table. Razumihin and Raskolnikov sat opposite Pulcheria Alexandrovna—Razumihin beside Luzhin, Raskolnikov next to his sister.

A moment's silence followed. Pyotr Petrovitch deliberately drew out a cambric handkerchief reeking of perfume and blew his nose with the air of a benevolent man who has been slighted and is firmly resolved to demand an explanation. In the passage it had occurred to him to keep his coat on and leave, thereby giving the two ladies a sharp and emphatic lesson about the gravity of the situation. But he couldn't bring himself to do it. Besides, he didn't like uncertainty, and he wanted answers. If his request had been so openly defied, something lay behind it, and he'd better find out what. He could always punish them later.
"I trust you had a pleasant journey?" he inquired stiffly of Pulcheria Alexandrovna.
"Oh yes, Pyotr Petrovitch."
"I'm gratified to hear it. And Avdotya Romanovna is not too fatigued?"
"I'm young and strong—I don't tire easily. But it was a great strain for mother," Dounia answered.

"That's inevitable, I'm afraid. Our national railways are terribly long. 'Mother Russia,' as they say, is a vast country. Despite my desire to do so, I was unable to meet you yesterday. But I trust everything went smoothly?"

"Oh no, Pyotr Petrovitch, it was all terribly distressing," Pulcheria Alexandrovna hastened to declare with a particular emphasis. "And if Dmitri Prokofitch hadn't been sent to us, I truly believe, by God Himself, we would have been utterly lost. Here he is! Dmitri Prokofitch Razumihin," she added, introducing him to Luzhin.
"I had the pleasure yesterday," Pyotr Petrovitch muttered, casting a hostile sidelong glance at Razumihin. Then he scowled and fell silent.

Pyotr Petrovitch belonged to that class of persons who appear very polite in society and make a great point of propriety, but who, the moment they're crossed, lose all composure and become more like sacks of flour than elegant men of the world. Again everyone was silent. Raskolnikov remained stubbornly mute; Avdotya Romanovna was unwilling to break the silence prematurely; Razumihin had nothing to say. So Pulcheria Alexandrovna grew anxious again.
"Marfa Petrovna is dead—have you heard?" she began, resorting to her main topic of conversation.

"To be sure, I heard. I was informed immediately, and in fact I've come to let you know that Arkady Ivanovitch Svidrigaïlov set out for Petersburg in great haste right after his wife's funeral. So at least I have on excellent authority."
"To Petersburg? Here?" Dounia asked in alarm, glancing at her mother.
"Yes, precisely—and no doubt with some design, considering the haste of his departure and all the circumstances preceding it."
"Good heavens! Won't he leave Dounia in peace even here?" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna.

"I imagine neither you nor Avdotya Romanovna need be alarmed, unless of course you yourselves wish to have some contact with him. For my part, I'm on my guard, and I'm currently tracking down where he's staying."

"Oh, Pyotr Petrovitch, you can't imagine how frightened I am!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna went on. "I've only seen him twice, but I thought him dreadful, dreadful! I'm convinced he was the cause of Marfa Petrovna's death."

"It's impossible to be certain about that. I have reliable information. I won't deny that he may have hastened the course of events by the moral influence of his affront, so to speak. But as to the general conduct and moral character of that individual, I share your opinion. I don't know whether he's well off now, or exactly what Marfa Petrovna left him—that I'll learn very shortly. But certainly here in Petersburg, if he has any money at all, he'll immediately lapse into his old ways. He's the most depraved and utterly vicious specimen of that class of men. I have good reason to believe that Marfa Petrovna, who was so unfortunate as to fall in love with him and pay off his debts eight years ago, was of service to him in another way as well. Solely through her efforts and sacrifices, a criminal case involving grotesque and homicidal brutality—for which he might easily have been sent to Siberia—was hushed up. That's the sort of man he is, if you care to know."
"Good heavens!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna. Raskolnikov listened attentively.
"Are you speaking the truth? Do you have solid evidence for this?" Dounia asked sternly and pointedly.

"I'm only repeating what Marfa Petrovna told me in confidence. I should note that from a legal standpoint the case was far from clear. There was, and I believe still is, a certain woman living here called Resslich, a foreigner, who lent small sums at interest and had other dealings. Svidrigaïlov had longstanding, close, and mysterious relations with this woman. She had a relative—a niece, I believe—living with her, a deaf-mute girl of fifteen or perhaps younger. Resslich hated this girl and grudged her every crust; she beat her mercilessly. One day the girl was found hanging in the attic. The verdict was suicide. After the usual proceedings, the matter was closed. But later, information surfaced that the child had been cruelly violated by Svidrigaïlov. True, this was not established conclusively. The information came from another German woman of loose character whose testimony was unreliable. No formal statement was made to the police, thanks to Marfa Petrovna's money and efforts. It remained gossip. But the story is very significant. You heard, no doubt, Avdotya Romanovna, when you were with them, the story of the servant Philip, who died of ill treatment six years ago, before the abolition of serfdom."
"I heard, on the contrary, that Philip hanged himself."
"Quite so. But what drove him—or perhaps disposed him—to suicide was the systematic persecution and cruelty of Mr. Svidrigaïlov."

"I don't know that," Dounia answered drily. "I only heard a strange story that Philip was a sort of hypochondriac, a 'domestic philosopher,' as the servants put it, who 'read himself silly,' and that he hanged himself partly because of Mr. Svidrigaïlov's mockery rather than his beatings. When I was there, he treated the servants well, and they were actually fond of him, though they did blame him for Philip's death."

"I see, Avdotya Romanovna, that you seem suddenly disposed to defend him," Luzhin observed, twisting his lips into an ambiguous smile. "No doubt he's an astute man, very insinuating with women—of which Marfa Petrovna, who died so strangely, is a terrible example. My only wish has been to be of service to you and your mother with my advice, given the renewed efforts we may certainly expect from him. For my part, I'm firmly convinced he'll end up in debtors' prison again. Marfa Petrovna had no intention of settling anything substantial on him, having her children's interests in mind, and if she left him anything, it would be the barest minimum—something insignificant and short-lived that wouldn't last a year for a man of his habits."
"Pyotr Petrovitch, I beg you," said Dounia, "say no more about Mr. Svidrigaïlov. It makes me miserable."
"He's just been to see me," Raskolnikov said, breaking his silence for the first time.
There were exclamations from everyone, and all eyes turned to him. Even Pyotr Petrovitch was startled.

"An hour and a half ago he came in while I was asleep, woke me, and introduced himself," Raskolnikov continued. "He was fairly cheerful and at ease, and quite expects us to become friends. He's especially anxious for an interview with you, Dounia, and asked me to help arrange it. He has a proposal for you, and he told me what it is. He also told me that a week before her death, Marfa Petrovna left you three thousand roubles in her will, Dounia, and that you can collect the money very soon."
"Thank God!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna, crossing herself. "Pray for her soul, Dounia!"
"It's a fact!" Luzhin blurted out.
"Tell us—what else?" Dounia urged Raskolnikov.
"Then he said he's not rich, that the estate was left to his children who are now with an aunt, that he's staying somewhere not far from me, but where exactly I don't know—I didn't ask."
"But what does he want to propose to Dounia?" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna in fright. "Did he tell you?"
"Yes."
"What was it?"
"I'll tell you later."
Raskolnikov stopped talking and turned to his tea.
Pyotr Petrovitch checked his watch.
"I'm afraid I have a business engagement, so I won't be in your way," he said with a slightly piqued air, and began getting up.
"Don't go, Pyotr Petrovitch," said Dounia. "You intended to spend the evening. Besides, you wrote that you wanted to have an explanation with mother."

"Precisely so, Avdotya Romanovna," Pyotr Petrovitch answered impressively, sitting down again but still holding his hat. "I certainly wished for an explanation with you and your honored mother on a very important point. But since your brother cannot speak openly about certain proposals from Mr. Svidrigaïlov in my presence, I too am unwilling to discuss certain matters of the greatest gravity in the presence of others. Moreover, my most important and earnest request has been disregarded."
Assuming an aggrieved air, Luzhin lapsed into dignified silence.

"Your request that my brother not be present was disregarded solely at my insistence," said Dounia. "You wrote that he had insulted you. I think this must be explained immediately and you two must be reconciled. If Rodya really has insulted you, then he should and will apologize."
Pyotr Petrovitch took a harder line.
"There are insults, Avdotya Romanovna, that no amount of goodwill can make one forget. There is a line in everything that it's dangerous to cross, and once crossed, there's no going back."

"That isn't exactly what I was talking about, Pyotr Petrovitch," Dounia interrupted with some impatience. "Please understand: our entire future depends on whether this can be cleared up and set right as quickly as possible. I'm telling you frankly from the start that I can't see it any other way, and if you have the slightest regard for me, this matter must be settled today, however difficult that may be. I repeat: if my brother is at fault, he will ask your forgiveness."

"I'm surprised you put it like that," Luzhin said, growing more and more irritated. "Esteeming and, so to speak, adoring you, I may very well be unable to tolerate certain members of your family. While I aspire to the happiness of your hand, I cannot accept obligations that are incompatible—"

"Oh, don't be so quick to take offense, Pyotr Petrovitch," Dounia interrupted with feeling, "and be the sensible and generous man I've always considered you. I've given you a great promise—I'm your fiancée. Trust me in this, and believe I can judge impartially. My taking on the role of judge is as much a surprise to my brother as to you. When I insisted that he come to today's meeting after receiving your letter, I told him nothing of my intentions. Understand: if you two can't be reconciled, I must choose between you—it's either you or him. That's how it stands on both sides. I mustn't make the wrong choice, and I mustn't. For your sake I'd have to break with my brother; for my brother's sake, with you. Right now I can find out for certain whether he truly is a brother to me, and I want to know. And about you—whether I'm dear to you, whether you value me, whether you're the right husband for me."

"Avdotya Romanovna," Luzhin declared huffily, "your words carry too much weight—indeed they are offensive, considering the position I have the honor to occupy in relation to you. To say nothing of your strange and insulting comparison, putting me on the same level as an insolent boy, you admit the possibility of breaking your promise. You say 'you or he,' thereby showing how little I mean to you. I cannot let this pass, given the relationship and obligations between us."
"What!" Dounia cried, flushing. "I set your interests beside everything I've held most precious in my life, everything that has been my whole life, and you complain that I make too little of you?"

Raskolnikov smiled sarcastically. Razumihin fidgeted. But Pyotr Petrovitch did not accept the rebuke. On the contrary, with every word he grew more obstinate and irritable, as though he was enjoying it.

"Love for the future partner of your life, for your husband, should outweigh your love for your brother," he pronounced solemnly. "And in any case, I refuse to be placed on the same level. Although I said I wouldn't speak openly in your brother's presence, I now intend to ask your honored mother for a necessary explanation on a point that deeply concerns my dignity. Your son," he turned to Pulcheria Alexandrovna, "yesterday, in the presence of Mr. Razudkin—or, I think that's it? Forgive me, I've forgotten your surname"—he bowed politely to Razumihin—"insulted me by distorting something I said to you in private conversation over coffee: namely, that marriage to a poor girl who has experienced hardship is more advantageous from a conjugal standpoint than to one raised in luxury, because it's better for the moral character. Your son deliberately exaggerated the meaning of my words, made them sound ridiculous, and accused me of malicious intent, relying, as far as I could tell, on your letter to him. I shall be happy, Pulcheria Alexandrovna, if you can convince me I'm mistaken and thereby set my mind at ease. Kindly tell me the exact terms in which you repeated my words in your letter to Rodion Romanovitch."
"I don't remember," Pulcheria Alexandrovna faltered. "I wrote them as I understood them. I don't know how Rodya repeated them to you. Perhaps he exaggerated."
"He could not have exaggerated except at your prompting."
"Pyotr Petrovitch," Pulcheria Alexandrovna declared with dignity, "the proof that Dounia and I didn't take your words badly is the fact that we are here."
"Well said, mother," said Dounia approvingly.
"So it's my fault again," Luzhin said, aggrieved.
"Well, Pyotr Petrovitch, you keep blaming Rodion, but you yourself just wrote something false about him," Pulcheria Alexandrovna added, growing bolder.
"I don't recall writing anything false."

"You wrote," Raskolnikov said sharply, not turning toward Luzhin, "that I gave money yesterday not to the widow of the man who was killed, as was actually the case, but to his daughter—whom I'd never seen before yesterday. You wrote this to create a rift between me and my family, and for that purpose added crude remarks about the character of a girl you don't know. All of that is mean slander."

"Excuse me, sir," Luzhin said, trembling with fury. "I elaborated on your qualities and conduct in my letter solely in response to your sister's and mother's inquiries about how I found you and what impression you made on me. As for what you've referred to, kindly point out one word of falsehood—show me that you didn't throw your money away, or that there aren't worthless people in that family, however unfortunate."
"In my opinion, you with all your virtues aren't worth the little finger of that unfortunate girl you're throwing stones at."
"Would you go so far, then, as to let her associate with your mother and sister?"
"I've already done so, if you care to know. I had her sit down today with mother and Dounia."
"Rodya!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna. Dounia turned crimson. Razumihin knitted his brows. Luzhin smiled with lofty sarcasm.

"You see for yourself, Avdotya Romanovna," he said, "whether agreement between us is possible. I hope this question is now settled once and for all. I shall withdraw, so as not to intrude on the pleasures of family intimacy and the sharing of secrets." He got up and reached for his hat. "But in withdrawing, I venture to request that in the future I be spared such meetings and, so to speak, compromises. I appeal particularly to you, honored Pulcheria Alexandrovna, especially since my letter was addressed to you and to no one else."
Pulcheria Alexandrovna was somewhat offended.

"You seem to think we're completely under your authority, Pyotr Petrovitch. Dounia has told you why your wish was disregarded—her intentions were the best. And the tone of your letter was rather like issuing orders. Are we to treat your every wish as a command? Let me tell you, on the contrary: you should be showing us particular consideration right now, because we've given up everything and come here relying on you, so in a sense we're already in your hands."

"That's not quite fair, Pulcheria Alexandrovna, especially at the present moment, when the news of Marfa Petrovna's bequest has arrived—which seems very timely, judging by the new tone you're taking with me," he added sarcastically.
"Judging from that remark, we may certainly conclude you were counting on our helplessness," Dounia observed icily.

"But I certainly cannot count on it now. And in particular, I wouldn't want to interfere with the discussion of the secret proposals of Arkady Ivanovitch Svidrigaïlov, which he has entrusted to your brother and which, I gather, hold great—and perhaps very agreeable—interest for you."
"Good heavens!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna.
Razumihin could no longer sit still.
"Aren't you ashamed now, sister?" Raskolnikov asked.
"I am ashamed, Rodya," said Dounia. "Pyotr Petrovitch, go away," she turned to him, white with anger.

Pyotr Petrovitch had clearly not expected this outcome. He had placed too much faith in himself, in his power, and in the helplessness of his victims. He couldn't believe it, even now. He turned pale, and his lips quivered.
"Avdotya Romanovna, if I walk out that door now, after such a dismissal, then you may be sure I will never come back. Think carefully. My word is final."
"What insolence!" Dounia cried, springing from her seat. "I don't want you to come back!"

"What! So that's how it is!" Luzhin exclaimed, unable to believe in the rupture until the very last moment, completely thrown off his calculations. "So that's how it is! But do you realize, Avdotya Romanovna, that I could protest?"

"What right have you to speak to her like that?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna burst out. "What could you possibly protest? What rights do you have? Am I to give my Dounia to a man like you? Go away, leave us alone! We're to blame for agreeing to a bad arrangement, and I most of all!"
"But you bound yourself, Pulcheria Alexandrovna," Luzhin raged, "by your promise, and now you're going back on it! Besides, I was led into expenses on that account—"
This last complaint was so characteristic of Pyotr Petrovitch that Raskolnikov, pale with anger and the effort of containing it, couldn't help laughing. But Pulcheria Alexandrovna was furious.

"Expenses? What expenses? Are you talking about our trunk? But the conductor carried it free, as a favor to you! Mercy, we bound you? Think about it, Pyotr Petrovitch—it was you who bound us hand and foot, not the other way around!"
"Enough, mother, please!" Avdotya Romanovna implored. "Pyotr Petrovitch, please be so kind as to leave."

"I'm going, but one last word," he said, now entirely unable to control himself. "Your mother seems to have completely forgotten that I resolved to take you, so to speak, after the gossip about your reputation had spread all over the district. In disregarding public opinion for your sake and restoring your reputation, I certainly had a right to expect fitting gratitude, even to look for it. And only now have my eyes been opened! I see that I may indeed have acted very, very recklessly in disregarding the general verdict—"
"Does this man want his head bashed in?" Razumihin cried, jumping up.
"You're a mean and spiteful man!" Dounia cried.
"Not a word! Not a move!" Raskolnikov said, holding Razumihin back. Then he walked right up to Luzhin. "Kindly leave this room," he said quietly and distinctly, "and not another word, or—"

Pyotr Petrovitch stared at him for several seconds, his pale face working with rage. Then he turned and walked out. Rarely has any man left a room carrying such vindictive hatred in his heart as he felt toward Raskolnikov. He blamed him, and him alone, for everything. It's worth noting that even as he went down the stairs, he still imagined his case might not be entirely lost, and that, as far as the ladies were concerned, things might 'very well indeed' be set right again.
